# MultiDatePick - Full Reference

> MultiDatePick is a no-code, Salesforce-native Lightning Web Component suite. An admin builds a calendar in a guided Setup Wizard, drops it on a page or Flow by pasting a Config Name, and every pick saves as a real record on their own object: no Apex, no Flow loop, no developer. It puts calendar, scheduling, and resource-booking interfaces into Flows, Lightning Record Pages, App Pages, Home Pages, and Experience Sites. Three components share a configurable base: Dates for multi-date selection with ranges and recurring patterns; Dates & Times for date plus per-date or shared time-slot scheduling with conflict detection; and Resource Booking for resource reservation with capacity tracking, live availability badges, business hours per resource, multi-resource checkboxes, bulk inline edit mode, and booking rules (minimum notice, a rolling book-ahead window and buffer time between bookings), plus an Add to Calendar file (.ics) after every save. The suite ships 130+ configurable settings (Dates 80+, Dates & Times 100+, Resource Booking 110+), six storage shapes (per-date, per-range, per-time-block, parent + sub-blocks, per-resource × date), status-color theming on any picklist, additive-only auto-save, a guided Setup Wizard with JSON import/export and Smart Field Mapping, pre-built configurations, and built-in translations for 9 languages.

---

## No-code setup

Is MultiDatePick no-code? Yes. A Salesforce admin sets it up with clicks in three steps:

1. Build a configuration in the Setup Wizard: say where the calendar lives and the shape of your records, and it picks the component and fills in the fields. Every object and field is a dropdown, Smart Field Mapping offers your own field names, and a live preview shows the result. Or import one of 41 ready-made configurations from the Config Library.
2. Drop the component on a record, App or Home page in Lightning App Builder, on a Screen Flow screen in Flow Builder, or on an Experience Cloud page, and paste the Config Name. Every other setting comes from the configuration.
3. Every pick saves as a real record. On a record page, or with Parent Record Id set in a Flow, Dates and Dates & Times save their own child records; Resource Booking always saves its own bookings. No Flow loop, no Apex.

Optional, for teams that want it: Flow outputs and the Parse Date Entries from JSON action for full control of what gets saved, and configurations as Custom Metadata for CI/CD.

## MultiDatePick: No-Code Salesforce Calendar and Booking (/index.html)

Marketing home page. Headline: "The no-code Salesforce calendar for dates, times and bookings."

- Problem it solves: standard Salesforce stores one date or one start and end range. MultiDatePick picks many dates, ranges, recurring patterns and per-date times on one calendar and writes the child records.
- Trust: passed the Salesforce AppExchange Security Review. 100% native: data stays in Salesforce, no external servers, no callouts.
- Three components in one package: Dates (many dates, ranges, recurring patterns, status colors), Dates & Times (adds a time slot grid and conflict checks), Resource Booking (rooms, equipment or people with availability, capacity and business hours).
- Five views of the same records: Calendar (month), Timeline (resources down, dates across, multi-day bars, drag to reschedule), Week (by hour), Utilization (booked of capacity heatmap), Agenda (next 60 days). Each placement picks its default view and which views users can switch to. Point the resource at User to schedule people.
- Standout features: recurring patterns (week intervals and monthly occurrences), status colors from any picklist, edit mode (status, date, time, resource, delete), capacity badges and conflict detection on save, drag to reschedule, status filter pills, hover popovers, date range consolidation, two-month view, time slots at any interval (15, 30 or 60 minutes are typical), 9 languages, WCAG 2.1 AA with a VPAT 2.5. 100+ properties across the suite (Dates 60+, Dates & Times 90+, Resource Booking 100+).
- Six record shapes, picked in the Setup Wizard: one per date, one per date range, one per time block, a parent plus sub-blocks for the gaps, single-resource booking, one per resource per date block.
- Setup Wizard with Walk me through it (three questions) or Configure all properties; 40+ importable configs in the Config Library; Smart Field Mapping for differently named fields. The free trial includes guided flows: Intro to MultiDatePick and a Deep Dive flow each for Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking.
- Runs on Screen Flows, Record Pages, App Pages, Home Pages and Experience Cloud sites. Editions: Enterprise, Unlimited, Performance, Developer and Salesforce Platform, plus industry clouds (Essentials and Professional are not supported).
- Pricing: $20/user/month, one plan with every feature, 30-day free trial, no card required. Coming soon to the Salesforce AppExchange.
- Live demo: a public ACME Financial advisor booking site, no login, resets every hour.

## Set Up MultiDatePick in Salesforce: Getting Started (/gettingstarted.html)

Five-step no-code setup guide, one GIF per step. No code required.

- Which component: Dates for dates only, Dates & Times for dates plus a time grid and conflict detection, Resource Booking for rooms, equipment or people with availability, capacity and business hours. All three ship in one package, every feature included.
- 1. Install from the AppExchange listing (at launch) for admins, all users or specific profiles. The components appear in Lightning App Builder and Flow Builder as Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking.
- 2. Assign a permission set: MultiDatePick - Setup (admins who build configs, includes the Setup Wizard), MultiDatePick - User (everyone who uses the calendars), MultiDatePick - All Access (both), or MultiDatePick - Guest for public-site guests. Users also need access to your own objects and fields.
- 3. Build a config in the Setup Wizard: say where the calendar lives and the shape of your records, and it picks the component and fills in the fields, with a live preview. Every object and field is a dropdown. Or import a ready-made config from the Config Library.
- 4. Lightning pages: drag the component on in Lightning App Builder and paste the Config Name. Record pages supply the parent record; App, Home and Experience pages also need Static Parent Record Id.
- 5. Screen Flow: drag the component onto a screen and set Config Name; every checkbox comes from the config. Bind Parent Record Id and every component saves its own records, no Loop needed (Resource Booking always saves its own bookings). For full control, leave Parent Record Id blank on Dates or Dates & Times and use the Flow outputs with the Parse Date Entries from JSON action.
- The package ships guided flows: Intro to MultiDatePick and a Deep Dive flow each for Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking, started from the Setup Wizard.

## No-Code Salesforce Multi-Date and Range Picker LWC (/multidatepickdates.html)

The Dates component: a no-code multi-date picker and date range picker for Salesforce Screen Flows, Record, App and Home pages and Experience Cloud sites, set up in the Setup Wizard.

- A standard Salesforce Date field holds one date; Dates saves every picked date as a related child record, so a record can hold any number of dates, each with its own status.
- Three ways to pick, mixable in one selection: click single dates, drag across days for a range, or Add Recurring Pattern (weekdays, weekends or custom days; every N weeks; 1st to 4th or last occurrence in the month; start and end date).
- Record shapes: one record per date, or one record per date range when End Date Field API Name is set (Mon to Fri becomes one record). Saving never deletes existing records.
- Any object, no code: pick your object and fields from dropdowns in the Setup Wizard (Child Object, Date Field, Relationship Field, optional End Date, Status, Hover Popover Fields, Blocked Dates Object).
- Features: status colors from any picklist, two-month view, Edit Mode (change status, move or delete saved dates in bulk), hover popovers, blocked dates from any object, earliest and latest date, Max Dates Allowed, Pre-Selected Dates, a second picklist on save, auto-named records.
- Five views of the same records: Calendar, Timeline (a date range draws as one bar), Week, Utilization (heatmap of records per day) and Agenda.
- Placement: paste the Config Name. Record pages use the page record as parent; App, Home and Experience pages also need Static Parent Record Id. In a Screen Flow, bind Parent Record Id and it saves its own records; or use Selected Dates and Date Ranges JSON outputs for full control.
- 80+ settings. Passed the Salesforce AppExchange Security Review; 100% native, data stays in Salesforce. $20/user/month with every component, 30-day free trial.

## Dates & Times: Salesforce Date and Time Slot Picker (/multidatepickdatetime.html)

- The Dates & Times component is a no-code calendar time slot picker: users pick many dates on one calendar, then pick times underneath, and every time block saves as a record on their own Salesforce child object. Set up in the Setup Wizard.
- Time Display Mode: grid (clickable slots, drag to select a block) or dropdown (start and end time pickers), at any interval (15, 30 or 60 minutes are typical). Earliest and Latest Time set the day's range.
- Shared or per-date times: one shared grid applies the same hours to every selected date, or Allow Different Times Per Date gives every date its own grid or dropdown.
- Conflict detection: Conflict Behavior block (taken times cannot be picked, and the save refuses a time taken meanwhile), skip (save the open times, name the taken ones) or allow.
- Group Time Slots by Period, status colors on dates and slots, Consolidate Time Span with break sub-blocks, Time Grid Only for one implied date, and whole-day saves with no times.
- Five views: Calendar, Week, Agenda, Timeline and Utilization. Also recurring patterns, Edit Mode, hover fields, blocked dates from any object, auto-named records, 9 languages.
- Saving: set Config Name and Parent Record Id (or place it on a record page) and it saves every record itself; no Loop, no Apex. For full control, leave Parent Record Id blank in a Flow and use Dates With Times JSON with the Parse Date Entries from JSON action.
- 100+ settings. Passed the Salesforce AppExchange Security Review; 100% native, data stays in Salesforce. $20/user/month with every component, 30-day free trial.

## No-Code Salesforce Booking Calendar and Resource Scheduler (/salesforce-booking-calendar.html)

The Resource Booking component: a no-code Salesforce booking calendar and resource scheduler on your own objects, set up in the Setup Wizard. It always saves its own bookings.

- Any object can be the resource: rooms, desks, vehicles, equipment, or User for people scheduling. Bookings save as records on your own booking object, linked to the resource and a parent record. No new data model, no Apex.
- Pick a resource, one or many dates, and open time slots at any interval, then Book. Adjacent slots join into one booking.
- Capacity: a Capacity Field on the resource keeps slots open until full, with live booked-of-capacity badges. Conflict Behavior block, skip or allow, checked again inside the save. Buffer time between bookings, minimum notice and a rolling booking window.
- Multi-resource booking, business hours per resource, blocked dates from a closures object (whole or part day, all or one resource, with the reason shown), status colors from any picklist, hover fields, Edit Mode (move, retime, reassign or cancel in bulk), a resource filter, Add to Calendar (.ics) after saving.
- Five views: Calendar, Timeline (resources down, dates across, drag to reschedule), Week, Utilization (booked-of-capacity heatmap) and Agenda.
- Placement: paste the Config Name in Lightning App Builder or Flow Builder. In a Screen Flow, bind Parent Record Id: the calendar saves each booking to that record, and with it empty it shows a setup message and books nothing. Experience Cloud self-service booking for guests and members.
- Editions: Enterprise, Unlimited, Performance, Developer and Salesforce Platform, plus industry clouds. 110+ settings, 9 languages. Passed the Salesforce AppExchange Security Review; 100% native, data stays in Salesforce. $20/user/month with every component, 30-day free trial.

## Config Library: Ready-to-Import Configs (/configlibrary.html)

41 ready-to-import configs across Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking, each with its default view and switcher views chosen. Each card lists its key settings by admin label (API name secondary) and one button, Copy for Setup Wizard: paste it into the Setup Wizard's Import / Export tab (Smart Field Mapping matches any object or field names that differ in your org), save, then use its Config Name wherever you place the component (Lightning page, Experience site, or Flow screen). For flows that save one record per date or shift, see the Flow loops post (/blog/salesforce-flow-loop-multiple-records.html). A three-question filter mirrors the wizard: capture times?, resource picker?, consolidate adjacent dates?

## MultiDatePick on App, Home & Experience Pages (/home-app-experience.html)

Guide to placing MultiDatePick on App Pages, Home Pages and Experience Sites using the Static Parent Record Id property.

- App Pages, Home Pages and Experience Sites have no automatic recordId, so Static Parent Record Id points the calendar at a specific parent record.
- The Save button appears only when all four are set: parent record (recordId, or Static Parent Record Id), Child Object API Name, Date Field API Name and Relationship Field API Name. A Config Name from the Setup Wizard supplies the last three.
- App and Home Pages are built in Lightning App Builder; Experience Sites in Experience Builder. Internal users need the MultiDatePick - User permission set.
- Static Parent Record Id points everyone at the same parent (public booking page, one org-wide calendar, fixed dashboard anchor). When the parent is chosen at runtime (Get Records on $User.Id, a ?id= URL parameter, or pick-first), use a Screen Flow and bind Parent Record Id. On guest sites $User does not apply.
- Public guest site checklist: (1) guest Read and Create on each object, never Edit or Delete; (2) field-level security, Read on shown fields and Edit on written fields; (3) a guest Read sharing rule, external org-wide default Private, Recalculate after a metadata deploy; (4) Apex class access to MultiDatePickController; (5) publish and activate. Also a default record owner for guest records, and guest Read on referenced resource or parent records (prefer custom objects over Contact/Account).
- Six patterns: internal booking hub, customer self-service scheduling, personal availability, event and cohort registration, volunteer and shift sign-up, project milestones.
- Existing Dates Mode = readonly turns a Home Page widget into a read-only view.

## Salesforce Screen Flow Guide (/flowcheatsheet.html)

The Config Name path: save a config in the Setup Wizard (or import one from the Config Library), add a Screen to a Screen Flow, drag on the MultiDatePick component, set Config Name, Save and Debug. Every checkbox comes from the config. To save against a record, bind Parent Record Id (in a Flow; on App, Home and Experience pages it is Static Parent Record Id). Outputs: Resource Booking gives Successful Bookings Count and Conflict Dates; Dates gives Selected Dates and Date Ranges JSON; Dates & Times gives Dates With Times JSON. To create records from JSON, use the Parse Date Entries from JSON Flow action, loop its entries, and create one record per entry. No Apex required. Appendix: manual mapping by label (Resource Object API Name, Resource Name Field, Capacity Field, Booking Object API Name, Booking Date/Start Time/End Time Fields, Booking Resource Field, Conflict Behavior block/skip/allow, Parent Record Id, Parent Record Relationship Field).

## User Guide (/user-guide.html)

Admin guide to MultiDatePick. Three components: Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking (in App Builder: MultiDatePick - Dates, MultiDatePick - Dates & Times and MultiDatePick - Resource Booking). The Setup Wizard has two start paths (Walk me through it, Configure all properties) plus Existing Configurations and Import / Export tabs, and five steps: Name & Type, Object & Fields, Time Fields, Status & Display, Review & Save. It names six record shapes: one record per date, per date range, per time block, parent plus sub-blocks, single resource, multiple resources. Permission sets: MultiDatePick - Setup (admins; includes the Setup Wizard), MultiDatePick - User (everyone who uses calendars), MultiDatePick - All Access (both); users also need object, field and record access to your own objects. Click to Save needs Child Object API Name, Date Field API Name, Relationship Field API Name and a parent (Parent Record Id in a Flow, Static Parent Record Id on App, Home and Experience pages). In a Screen Flow set Config Name; every checkbox comes from the config. Five views: Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization (read only), Agenda (read only). Time Interval (Minutes) accepts any interval; 15, 30 or 60 minutes are typical. Capacity needs both booking time fields. Closures block whole days, hours or one resource. Guest pages need object permissions, field security, a guest sharing rule (external default Private, Recalculate after a metadata deploy), Apex class access to MultiDatePickController on the guest profile, and an activated site. Flow recipes are no-code (Parse Date Entries from JSON, Roll-Up Summary or a Record-Triggered Flow). Includes a searchable reference of 100+ properties by label and API name.

## Accessibility & VPAT 2.5 | MultiDatePick (/accessibility.html)

VPAT 2.5 self-attested conformance report against WCAG 2.1 A/AA, Revised Section 508, and EN 301 549 V3.2.1.

- Product version: managed package 0.12.0-4. Report date and last verified: October 21, 2026, on the managed package install and on the unpackaged source.
- Scope: the Dates, Dates & Times and Resource Booking components, the five calendar views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda) and the Setup Wizard. Salesforce's own page chrome is covered by Salesforce's VPAT.
- Method: axe-core 4.11 (WCAG 2.1 A and AA rules) scoped to the MultiDatePick component, plus code review of ARIA roles, names and keyboard handling.
- Scan results: zero violations on all eight surfaces. Rules passed: Dates 16, Dates & Times 17, Resource Booking 17, Calendar view 18, Timeline 17, Week 17, Utilization 17, Agenda 16.
- Two checks flagged for manual review everywhere: ARIA id references inside Lightning's shadow DOM (ids confirmed in code), and contrast, which axe could not compute inside the component.
- Calendar uses ARIA grid markup with aria-selected; the view switcher is a labeled button group with aria-pressed; every booking bar, week block, heatmap cell and agenda row is a native button with an accessible name.
- Partially Supports: 1.4.3 Contrast (admins choose status colors) and 1.4.10 Reflow (Timeline, Week and Utilization scroll horizontally in narrow containers).
- 9 languages honoring the user's Salesforce Locale.
- Related: Section 508 guide for government teams at /blog/salesforce-section-508-government-calendar.html.

## Salesforce Add to Calendar: Bookings Into Outlook and Google (/blog/salesforce-add-to-calendar.html)

Give every Salesforce booking an Add to Calendar button: one .ics file for Outlook, Google and Apple Calendar after Save, even for Experience Cloud guests. No code.

A booking saved in Salesforce is only half done until it is in the person's own calendar. Turn on Show Add to Calendar After Saving and every successful save offers an Add to Calendar button that downloads one .ics calendar file with an event for each record just saved: the record name as the title, the saved date and times (date-only records as all-day events, a range as one event), the resource as the location, the status as the description and the Salesforce record Id as the unique ID. It opens in Outlook, Google Calendar and Apple Calendar; when a browser cannot create the file, a single booking gets an Add to Google Calendar link. The file is built in the browser, so it works for guests on public Experience Cloud booking pages, and it needs no connected app, OAuth or outbound callout: MultiDatePick stays 100% native. It is a one-time file rather than a live sync, so a booking that moves later needs a fresh file. Setup is one checkbox on the component or the Setup Wizard config.

## The Salesforce Account Calendar: Every Related Record in One View (/blog/salesforce-calendar-related-records.html)

Show tasks and records from contacts, opportunities and custom objects on one Salesforce account calendar. One Rollup Field, up to five lookups deep, no Apex.

- Published October 31, 2026.
- The problem: a calendar on a record page normally loads only the records that look up to that record (one level). On an Account page with a Task calendar that is the tasks whose Related To is the account; tasks logged on the account's contacts and opportunities are left out, and so are grandchild records of custom objects.
- Rollup Field (component property rollupField; Setup Wizard Fields screen, "Also" box): a second field, or a path through lookups, that also leads back to the page record. The calendar shows every record that matches the Relationship Field API Name OR the Rollup Field.
- New records still save through the Relationship Field API Name. Rollup Field only widens what the calendar shows.
- Paths use Salesforce relationship notation, up to five levels: AccountId, Project__r.Account__c, Location__r.Region__r.Account__c, Quote__r.OpportunityId.
- Example from the post (Northwind Logistics demo account): a Task calendar saved through WhatId showed 4 marked days in November with the account's own tasks; with Rollup Field AccountId it showed 11, adding the contact's calls and the opportunity's milestones.
- Records load as the viewing user, so record sharing and field-level security apply.
- Components: Dates and Dates & Times, for any standard or custom object. The Resource Booking component uses Rollup Field with This Record Only, so its Timeline, Week, Utilization and Agenda views show the bookings tied to the page record through the lookup path.
- Setup: Setup Wizard > Account record page > one record per date > Fields: Task, Relationship Field API Name Related To ID (WhatId), Date Field API Name ActivityDate, Rollup Field AccountId > save a Config Name > add the Dates component to the Account page with that Config Name.
- Use cases: account managers, field service (site visits per location), project delivery, customer success, nonprofits (household members), property management (unit inspections rolled up through the building).

## Salesforce Campaign Dates: Every Event Day, No Apex (/blog/salesforce-campaign-multiple-dates.html)

Track every date of a Salesforce Campaign on one calendar: tour stops, webinar series and volunteer days saved as child records, with status colors. No Apex.

A Campaign has one start date and one end date. Your tour, webinar series or volunteer program has many. Put them all on the Campaign record, each one a real record with a status, without writing Apex.
"How do I add more than one date to a Salesforce Campaign?" "Where do I track each stop of the roadshow?" "Which webinar sessions are confirmed?" A Campaign only knows when it starts and ends. Everything in between ends up in a spreadsheet or a long description field.
MultiDatePick puts a calendar on the Campaign record page. Click the days, save, and each one becomes its own child record linked to the Campaign, colored by status. It works on Campaigns the same way it works on any object: by configuration. No Apex required.

### What you get on the Campaign page
- **Every date at a glance**
All of the Campaign's dates load onto the calendar when the record opens. No related list to scroll.
- **Status colors**
Planned, Confirmed, Completed, Cancelled: each status gets its own color, and the pills above the calendar filter by status.
- **Hover for details**
Point at a date to see the record behind it, such as the stop name, venue and status, with a link to open it.
- **Recurring patterns**
Every Tuesday for eight weeks is one pattern and one click. Handy for webinar series and send schedules.
- **Edit mode**
Select several dates, then change their status, move them to another day, or delete them in one step.
- **Real records**
Each date is a child record with a lookup to the Campaign. Report on it, build flows on it, share it like anything else.

### Set it up in three steps
The components are object-agnostic. They do not know or care that the parent is a Campaign; they need a child object to save into and a lookup that points back. That is the whole integration.
- Create the child object. In Object Manager, create a custom object such as Campaign Date. Give it a Lookup field to Campaign and a Date field. Add a Status picklist (Planned, Confirmed, Completed, Cancelled) and any detail fields you want on hover, such as Venue.
- Run the Setup Wizard. Open the MultiDatePick Setup Wizard tab and configure the Dates component. Pick Campaign Date as the object, the Campaign lookup as the relationship field and your Date field. On Status & Display, choose the status field, a color per value and the hover fields. Save the config under a name like Campaign_Dates.
- Drop the component on the Campaign page. Open any Campaign, click Edit Page, drag the MultiDatePick Dates component onto the layout and enter the config name in Config Name. Save and activate. Every Campaign now has its calendar.
Need times as well as days, like a webinar at 11:00 and a repeat at 3:00? Use the Dates & Times component instead and add Start and End Time fields to the child object. The steps are the same.

### Prefer a Screen Flow?
The same config works inside Flow. Add the Dates component to a screen and set Config Name; every setting comes from the config, with no checkboxes to set in Flow Builder. Pass the Campaign Id into Parent Record Id and the component saves the child records itself. Leave it blank if you would rather loop the Selected Dates output and create the records your own way. The multiple dates in a Screen Flow post walks through both patterns.

### What teams track on Campaigns
Anything a Campaign does on more than one day fits the same child object:

### The settings that shape it
Each one is a field in the Setup Wizard and a property on the component, so nothing here needs code:

### Questions people ask
Q: Can a Salesforce Campaign have multiple dates?
A standard Campaign has one Start Date and one End Date. To track every day of a tour, webinar series or volunteer program, add a small child object with a lookup to Campaign and put the MultiDatePick Dates component on the Campaign record page. Every date you click is saved as its own child record.
Q: Do I need Apex or a developer to add dates to Campaigns?
No. The child object and its fields are point-and-click in Object Manager, the Setup Wizard writes the calendar configuration, and the component goes on the page in Lightning App Builder. There is no Campaign-specific code to write or install.
Q: Where are the Campaign dates stored?
In your own custom object, for example Campaign Date, with one record per date and a lookup to the Campaign. They are ordinary Salesforce records, so list views, reports, flows and sharing all work on them as usual.
Q: Can each Campaign date have its own status?
Yes. Add a picklist such as Planned, Confirmed, Completed and Cancelled, choose a color for each value, and the calendar paints every date in its status color. Edit mode lets you select several dates and change their status, move them, or delete them in one step.
Q: Can I use it in a Screen Flow instead of the record page?
Yes. Add the Dates component to a flow screen and set Config Name to the config you saved in the Setup Wizard. Pass the Campaign Id into Parent Record Id and the component saves the child records itself, or leave it blank and loop the Selected Dates output.

## Salesforce Utilization Heatmap: See Who Is Overbooked (/blog/salesforce-utilization-heatmap.html)

A Salesforce utilization heatmap: each resource down the side, every day showing booked against capacity, overbooking flagged, one click into the schedule.

Every room, person or asset down the side, every day across the top, and each cell showing how much of its capacity is booked. A capacity dashboard for your own Salesforce objects, set up without code.
"Is the team overbooked next week?" "Which room sits empty most of the month?" "Can we take on one more engagement?" Those are capacity questions. A calendar shows what is booked; it does not show how full anything is. A utilization heatmap does.
MultiDatePick's Utilization view reads the same bookings as its calendar and timeline and turns them into a grid of fill levels: one row per resource, one cell per day, each cell saying how many of that resource's places are taken. It is one config field away from any placement, and it needs nothing more than a number on the resource for capacity.

### What the heatmap shows
- **Booked of capacity**
Each cell reads like 3/4: three of four places taken. The fuller the day, the darker the blue.
- **Overbooking flagged**
A day booked past capacity gets an orange ring. It is never quietly capped at "full".
- **Combined availability**
A row across the top shows the whole group's fill per day as a percentage, so the crunch days stand out.
- **Average and open**
The right-hand column gives each resource's average for the month and how many places are still open from today.
- **Click to drill in**
Click a booked cell and the component opens that resource's week on that day, ready to book or edit.
- **Works without capacity**
No capacity field yet? Cells show a plain count of bookings on the same scale, and the grid says so.

### A month of capacity in one look
Reports can tell you utilization, one question at a time. The heatmap shows the whole month at once, so patterns jump out that a report would never surface: the advisor who is full every Tuesday, the room nobody books on Fridays, the week where everyone is at capacity at the same time. The grid opens on today, keeps resource names pinned while you scroll, and counts open places only from today forward, because unused capacity last week cannot be booked anymore.

### Multi-day work counts on every day it runs
Capacity covers more than meetings. A consultant can carry two client engagements at a time; a crew can work one job site at once; a training room hosts one course for a whole week. The heatmap counts a multi-day booking on every day it covers, so an engagement that runs Monday to Friday fills all five cells. Set the capacity to the number of things a resource can carry at once and the grid shows exactly when each person is fully committed.

### Who uses a Salesforce utilization heatmap
The resource can be any object, so the same view answers capacity questions for very different teams:

### The settings that shape it
Every one of these is a property on the component and a field in the Setup Wizard, so nothing here needs code:

### Questions people ask
Q: How do I see resource utilization in Salesforce?
Standard Salesforce has no utilization view for your own booking objects; you would build a report per question. MultiDatePick adds a Utilization view to the calendar component: each resource is a row, each day a cell showing booked against that resource's capacity, with a combined row for the whole group and an average and open count on the right.
Q: What does a cell like 2/2 or 3/4 mean?
Bookings on that day against the resource's capacity. 3/4 means three of four places are taken. The darker the blue, the fuller the day, and a day booked past capacity gets an orange ring so it stands out.
Q: What if my resource object has no capacity field?
The heatmap still works. Cells show a plain count of bookings on the same blue scale, and a note under the grid says so. Add a number field for capacity whenever you want percentages and open places instead.
Q: Can I book or edit from the Utilization view?
Utilization is read only by design: it answers how full things are. Click any booked cell and the component opens that resource's week on that day, where you can book, move or edit.
Q: Can the rows be people instead of rooms?
Yes. The resource can be any object, including User. Add a capacity number to User and the heatmap becomes a team capacity dashboard: who is full, who has room, and which weeks are overloaded.

## Salesforce Timeline View: Every Resource on One Screen (/blog/salesforce-timeline-view.html)

A Salesforce resource timeline: rooms, people and equipment down the side, dates across, multi-day bookings as one bar, and drag to reschedule. No code.

Rooms, people, equipment or projects down the side, dates across the top, and every booking drawn as one bar. A resource timeline for any Salesforce object, set up without code.
"Which room is free next Tuesday?" "Who on the team has capacity this week?" "When does the van come back?" Each of those is a question about many resources across many days, and a month calendar answers it one resource at a time. A timeline answers it in one look.
MultiDatePick's Timeline view puts every resource on its own row and every booking on a bar that runs exactly as long as the booking does. It reads your own Salesforce objects, saves through the same path as the rest of the component, and is one config field away from any placement.

### What the timeline does that a calendar cannot
- **One bar per booking**
A booking that runs Monday to Friday is one continuous bar, so its length is visible at a glance.
- **Lanes for overlaps**
Overlapping bookings on a resource stack into lanes. A busy day collapses to a count you expand in place.
- **Capacity strip**
A strip above each group shows how full every day is against the resources' combined capacity.
- **Day, Week and Month zoom**
Hours across for today, two weeks for planning, a month for the long view. One click between them.
- **Drag to reschedule**
Slide a bar to move it, pull an edge to stretch it. It saves on release and stays where you put it.
- **Book from the grid**
Drag across empty days on a resource's row to select them, then book. The row picks the resource for you.

### Drag to reschedule, stretch to extend
Plans change, and changing one should not mean opening a record, editing two date fields and saving. On the timeline you grab the bar. Pull its right edge and the booking runs longer; grab the middle and it slides to other days. The bar shows the dates it will land on while you drag, saves the moment you let go, and stays in its lane with a brief highlight so you can see exactly what changed.
Switch to Day zoom and the columns become hours. The same gestures then move and stretch a booking's start and end times, so a meeting that runs over is one drag to fix.

### Capacity you can see at a glance
Above the rows, a capacity strip shades every day by how much of the resources' combined capacity is booked, so the crunch weeks stand out before anyone asks. Group rows by a picklist or lookup (building, team, region) and each group gets its own strip. When one resource has several bookings on the same day, they stack into lanes; a day with more than a few collapses to a count that expands in place when you click it.

### Who uses a Salesforce timeline
The resource can be any object, so the same view fits very different teams:

### The settings that shape it
Every one of these is a property on the component and a field in the Setup Wizard, so nothing here needs code:

### Questions people ask
Q: Does Salesforce have a timeline view for resources?
Not as a standard Lightning component for your own objects. Calendars in Salesforce show one person's events, and Gantt-style charts usually mean an add-on built for projects. MultiDatePick adds a resource timeline that reads any custom or standard object: pick the object that holds bookings and the object that holds resources, and every resource becomes a row.
Q: Can I drag bookings on the timeline to reschedule them?
Yes. With Edit Mode on, grab the middle of a bar to move it to other days or either edge to change its start or end. The bar shows its new dates while you drag and saves when you let go. In Day zoom the same gestures move and stretch the booking's start and end times.
Q: Can the rows be people instead of rooms?
Yes. The resource can be any object, including User. Point it at User and the timeline becomes a staff roster: each person a row, their shifts, visits or assignments as bars.
Q: How do I stop a long list of resources turning into a wall of rows?
Set Max View Resources to draw only the busiest rows, group rows under a picklist or lookup with Timeline Group By Field, and choose whether rows show all resources or only ones with bookings. Every resource still counts toward capacity; the settings only change what is drawn.
Q: Does the timeline work on Experience Cloud sites and record pages?
Yes. It is one of five views in the same component, so it runs anywhere the component does: record pages, app and home pages, Flow screens and Experience Cloud sites.

## Section 508 Calendar for Salesforce Government Orgs (/blog/salesforce-section-508-government-calendar.html)

State and local agencies now have until April 2027 to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. What that means for scheduling in Salesforce, and the accessible calendar built for it.

Agencies on Salesforce book inspections, appointments, facilities and field staff every day. The federal deadline for making those pages accessible just moved to April 2027. Here is what it asks of the calendar, and how MultiDatePick answers it.
In April 2024 the Department of Justice set a firm technical standard for state and local government websites and apps under ADA Title II: WCAG 2.1 Level AA. In April 2026 it gave agencies one more year to get there. That year is the window to fix the parts of your Salesforce org that residents and staff actually click, and the scheduling calendar is near the top of that list.

### The dates that apply now
An interim final rule published April 20, 2026 extended both compliance dates by one year. The standard itself did not change.
Two things are easy to miss. First, many articles still quote April 2026, which is out of date. Second, the Justice Department is explicit that the obligation to make services accessible did not pause: the dates set when the specific technical standard becomes enforceable, not when accessibility starts to matter. Federal agencies were never on this clock at all; they answer to Section 508, which already requires WCAG 2.0 AA, and every one of those criteria is also part of 2.1 AA.

### Where scheduling shows up in a government org
Almost every public service on Salesforce has a calendar in it.
- **Inspections**
Homeowners pick a day for a building or permit inspection.
- **Appointments**
Residents book licensing, benefits and records visits.
- **Facility rentals**
Families reserve pavilions, ballfields and community rooms.
- **Clinics**
Vaccination slots with a fixed number of seats per hour.
- **Field staff**
Inspectors, caseworkers and poll workers scheduled across a month.
- **Closures**
Meeting rooms blocked for holidays and maintenance.

### What MultiDatePick does, criterion by criterion
MultiDatePick was built to WCAG 2.1 AA from the start. This is what that looks like in the component your residents and staff actually use:
The VPAT marks two criteria as Partially Supports, and says exactly why. Contrast: the default palette meets 4.5:1, but admins can choose their own status colors, and a vendor cannot guarantee a color it did not pick. Reflow: at 320 pixels wide the month grid keeps its seven columns and narrows rather than stacking. Procurement reviewers trust a report that explains its partials over a wall of unexplained Supports.

### How it compares
Agencies usually weigh four ways to put a scheduling calendar in Salesforce. Only one of them gives you multi-date and resource booking, published accessibility documentation and resident data that never leaves your org, all on day one.
The standard date field is accessible, but it holds one date, so it cannot run a booking. An external tool can book, but residents' names, addresses and appointment history then live in someone else's system, which is a second security review and a second accessibility review. A custom build keeps the data home, but your team now owns the WCAG testing, the VPAT and every fix, forever. MultiDatePick is the only option on the list that clears every row.

### Built for how government buys
- 100% Salesforce native. No external servers, no outbound callouts, no subprocessors. Resident data stays in your org under the sharing and field-level security you already configured, so there is no new data processor to approve. See Trust & Security.
- Passed Salesforce's AppExchange security review. The managed package went through Salesforce's own review before listing.
- Resident self-service. The Resource Booking component runs on Experience Cloud sites, so residents can pick an inspection window or reserve a facility on the same accessible calendar staff use.
- No code to maintain. A Setup Wizard writes the configuration, with a live preview of the real component, so a small IT team is not signing up for a custom build it has to keep compliant.

### Getting ready before April 2027
- Inventory every date picker your public touches. Experience Cloud pages first, then staff Screen Flows. Note which ones are standard fields and which are third-party or custom components.
- Request a current VPAT for every third-party component. Check the report date and that it was tested on the packaged version you actually install.
- Test the booking path with a keyboard alone. Pick a date, choose a time, save. If you cannot finish without a mouse, neither can a resident who relies on a keyboard or a screen reader.

## Salesforce Calendar: What It Does and What It Leaves Out (/salesforce-calendar.html)

The built-in Salesforce Calendar (Lightning Experience) shows Events, plus coworker, public and resource calendars, in Day, Week and Month views, with a Table view that lists events. Users can build calendars from any object with a date or date/time field, filtered by a list view, and create recurring events as an event series. Day, week and month views show up to 150 or 500 items in total, depending on setup (Salesforce Help).

Where it stops: each record shows on one date or one start to end span; clicking a slot creates one Event, so there is no way to select a set of days and save them to a record; resource calendars show bookings but do not count capacity; the calendar lives on its own Calendar page; there is no resource timeline or capacity heatmap.

MultiDatePick picks up from there: click or drag any number of days on one calendar, recurring patterns (weekdays, weekends, custom days, every N weeks), a time slot for each date at any interval, resource booking with booked of capacity badges and a conflict check on save, and five views (Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization, Agenda). It runs on record, App and Home pages, Screen Flows and Experience Cloud sites, and writes your own child records. Keep the Salesforce Calendar for your own meetings and email sync; use MultiDatePick wherever a record needs many dates, times or bookings. $20/user/month, every feature, 30-day free trial; coming soon to the Salesforce AppExchange.

## Troubleshooting (/troubleshooting.html)

Each MultiDatePick setup message with a screenshot, the cause and a fix: no Save button, Wrong component and Configuration mismatch banners, the red could not load its data banner, Configuration Required, No resources available, Capacity needs both time fields, saved dates not showing, date limit reached, a Flow ignoring Config Name, and site members not seeing records. Access errors: assign MultiDatePick - User (users), MultiDatePick - Setup (admins, includes the Setup Wizard) or MultiDatePick - All Access (both). Insufficient privileges means no Read on the parent object or record; No read access to field means missing Read field-level security (admins too, for new custom fields); Time group failed to save or Insert failed means missing Edit on a field the save writes; INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_ON_CROSS_REFERENCE_ENTITY means no access to the parent or resource record; guests seeing an empty calendar usually need the sharing rule recalculated, MultiDatePickController class access and an activated site.

## Salesforce VPAT: What Admins Need to Know (/blog/salesforce-vpat-accessibility.html)

Published August 12, 2026, updated October 21, 2026.

- A VPAT is a vendor's self-assessment against accessibility standards, not a certificate.
- It covers WCAG 2.1 A and AA, Revised Section 508 (US public sector) and EN 301 549 (EU public sector).
- Conformance levels: Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable. A few honest Partially Supports entries are a good sign.
- Four questions for a vendor: when was it last verified and against which version; was the packaged version tested; automated, manual or both; is color ever the only signal.
- MultiDatePick's VPAT was verified October 21, 2026 against managed package 0.12.0-4, with zero axe-core violations across three components and five calendar views.

## Multiple Dates in a Salesforce Screen Flow (/blog/multiple-dates-in-a-salesforce-screen-flow.html)

How to capture many dates in one Salesforce Flow screen, and what to do with the collection afterwards. Loops, parsing and the limits of standard components.

Flow gives you one Date field per screen element. If someone needs to choose nine days, that is a problem. Here are the options, and the tradeoffs of each.
Every admin hits this eventually. A time-off request, an availability form, a training sign-up: the user needs to select several dates that are not necessarily consecutive, and Flow's standard Date component captures exactly one.

### The workarounds, and why they hurt
The start-and-end workaround is the most common and the most quietly wrong. "I need the 3rd, 4th, 11th and 18th off" becomes 3rd to 18th, which is sixteen days of implied absence. The data looks clean and is simply incorrect.

### The real fix: a screen component that returns a collection
What Flow actually needs is a screen component that lets the user click as many dates as they like and hands back a collection. Once you have that, the rest of the flow is ordinary: loop the collection, create a record per date, done.
MultiDatePick returns several outputs, depending on what you are capturing:

### Turning JSON back into records
Two of those outputs are JSON, because Flow has no native type for "a list of objects with several fields each." You do not parse text in a formula. The package ships a Flow action, Parse Date Entries from JSON, that takes the JSON and returns a proper collection with From Date, To Date, Start Time and End Time. You loop that collection like any other.

### One gotcha that costs people an hour
Want the component to save the records itself? Pass the parent record's Id into Parent Record Id and it creates one child record per date. Leave it blank to loop the output and create the records your own way.

### Decide the record shape before you build
The same nine selected dates can become nine records, or four records if consecutive days collapse into ranges, or one parent record with sub-blocks. Each is correct for a different report. Decide it before you build the flow, because changing it afterwards means migrating data as well as editing the flow.

## Prevent Double Booking in Salesforce: Conflicts & Capacity (/blog/prevent-double-booking-in-salesforce.html)

Validation rules fire after the user has already chosen. How to check availability before selection, and handle capacity where more than one booking fits.

Validation rules cannot see other records. That single limitation is why most Salesforce booking systems discover their conflicts a day late.
Double-booking is a timing problem. By the time anything in standard Salesforce can tell you the room is taken, the user has already chosen it, filled in the rest of the form, and moved on.

### Why the obvious tools do not work
They all share the same shape: reject the user after the choice. Even a correct custom solution produces "that slot is taken, please try again," which is a worse experience than never offering the slot.

### Overlap is not equality
Duplicate rules tempt people, so here is the rule. Two bookings conflict when one starts before the other ends and ends after the other starts. A booking from 9:00 to 10:00 and one from 9:30 to 10:30 overlap by half an hour while sharing no identical field values. Any approach based on matching values will miss it every time.

### Conflict and capacity are different problems
They often get treated as one thing.
- **A conflict**
Two things competing for a resource that holds one. A room, an interviewer, a vehicle.
- **Capacity**
A resource that holds several. The question is how many are left. A class with twenty seats, a shift needing four nurses, a desk zone with sixty spaces.
Treating a capacity resource as a conflict resource means you can never book the second person. Treating a conflict resource as capacity-of-one technically works but loses the counts you probably want to report on.

### Three sensible behaviors
"Block it" is not always right. When somebody selects twelve dates and two of them clash, rejecting the whole submission is hostile. Useful systems offer a choice:
- **Block**
Refuse the save and report the clash. Right when every date matters.
- **Skip**
Save the ten that are free, report the two that were not. Usually the humane default for bulk selection.
- **Allow**
Permit the overlap deliberately. Some businesses overbook on purpose.

### The real fix is earlier
Every mechanism above operates at save time. The fix is to move the check to selection time: query what already exists when the calendar loads, draw it onto the grid, and never offer a slot that is gone. Save-time checks still run as a backstop for the genuine race condition where two people are looking at the same free slot, but they stop being the primary defense.

## Recurring Date Patterns in Salesforce (/blog/recurring-date-patterns-in-salesforce.html)

Every Monday and Thursday for six weeks is a pattern a date range cannot hold. Recurring selection patterns in Salesforce, and how to get them without code.

Every other Tuesday. The 2nd and 4th Friday. The last Saturday of the month. These are ordinary business rules, and Salesforce has no field that expresses any of them.
Recurrence exists in Salesforce for Events and Tasks, and it stops there. The moment your schedule lives on a custom object (a shift, a session, an inspection, an on-call rotation), you are on your own, and the usual answer is that somebody works the dates out on a paper calendar and enters them by hand.

### The two kinds of recurrence people mean
They get conflated, and they need different logic.
Interval recurrence counts forward from a start date and does not care about month boundaries. Occurrence recurrence resets every month, and "last" is awkward because it lands on the 4th or 5th week depending on the month. That single word is where most hand-rolled implementations break.

### Why writing it yourself goes wrong
- **Month lengths vary**
"The 5th Monday" exists in some months and not others.
- **Leap years**
They quietly shift every calculation that assumes a fixed year.
- **"Every other week" needs an anchor**
Every other week starting when? Two people will disagree.
- **Weekends and holidays**
They may need skipping, and your holidays live in your own org data.
- **Generating too far ahead**
It creates thousands of records nobody asked for.
None of these are hard individually. Together they are a week of work and a permanent source of edge-case bugs.

### Generating dates instead of storing a rule
There is a design decision underneath the algorithm: do you store the rule and expand it at read time, or expand it once and store the resulting dates?
Storing dates is almost always the better answer in Salesforce. Concrete date records report, roll up, filter, and drive automation like any other data. A stored rule needs interpreting everywhere it is used, and Salesforce reporting cannot interpret it at all. The tradeoff is that changing the pattern means regenerating, which is why the pattern picker belongs at the point of entry rather than buried in configuration.

### The three patterns, on screen
Custom Day-of-Week comes first, because no standard field expresses it at all. Pick any combination of weekdays, set the interval, give it a range, and the calendar fills in every matching date before you save anything.
Weekdays and Weekends are the two shortcuts people reach for most, and they do the same expansion with one click.

### Let people see the dates before they commit
The best thing a recurrence UI can do is show its work. When the user picks "every 2 weeks on Tuesday" and immediately sees the actual dates highlighted on a calendar, mistakes get caught in the second before saving rather than the week after. It also settles the "every other week starting when" argument instantly, because the anchor is visible.
The same applies to consolidation. If your recurring selection produces Monday to Friday for six weeks, you may want thirty records or you may want six, one per week, with a start and end date. Deciding that at selection time is far cheaper than migrating afterwards.

## Configure a Salesforce Calendar Without Code (/blog/salesforce-calendar-setup-wizard.html)

100+ properties sounds like a project. It is a Setup Wizard, three questions about your records, and a live preview that renders the real Salesforce calendar.

100+ properties sounds like a project. It is a wizard, three questions, and a live preview that shows you the calendar before you save anything.
Most Salesforce components with real depth make you learn them twice: once to understand the properties, once to remember which combination you picked last time. The Setup Wizard exists so you do neither. It asks what you are scheduling, writes the configuration as metadata, and hands you a name you can use anywhere.

### Two ways in, plus two shortcuts
The Create New tab opens on two paths. Two more tabs sit beside it for configs you already have.
- **Walk me through it**
Three questions about what you are scheduling. Best for first-time setup.
- **Configure all properties**
Every property visible, with a live preview. Best when you know exactly what you want.
- **Existing Configurations**
Your saved configs with their component type. Open one to edit or clone it.
- **Import**
Paste a config from the Config Library or another org.

### Five steps, start to finish

### The three questions that decide everything
The guided path asks about the shape of the records you want, rather than about properties. Every answer combination is valid, and together they decide what the component writes:
- Do you need times, or just dates? Dates alone, a time on each date, or a parent block with sub-blocks for the gaps inside it.
- Are you booking a resource? None, one at a time, or several at once.
- Should consecutive dates collapse into a range? One record per date, or one record with a start and an end.
The answers are independent, so they describe the whole grid of possibilities rather than a menu of presets. Monday through Friday for six weeks can be thirty records or six. You choose that here, on purpose, before any data exists.

### A live preview, before anything is saved
The preview pane renders a working calendar underneath the form as you change properties. Turn on two-month view and it appears. Add status colors and the cells fill. It is the actual component, so what you approve is what you deploy.
The expensive mistakes in scheduling configuration are shape decisions you cannot see until real records exist. Seeing the calendar respond while you are still deciding removes most of that risk.

### Inside the steps: Object & Fields, Time Fields, Status & Display
Two steps do most of the heavy lifting on a booking or scheduling config. Time Fields maps the start time, end time and interval your calendar needs. Status & Display is where the visual polish lives, from status-driven cell colors to which fields show on hover.
On Status & Display, pick a status field, map a color to each value, and choose whether the color paints the calendar cell, the time slot grid, or both. Add hover fields so pointing at a booking previews the details.

### What it actually writes
Saving deploys a Custom Metadata record. Three things follow:
- It is deployable. Custom Metadata moves through your normal release pipeline, sandbox to production, like any other component.
- It is reusable. Put the name in Config Name on any component and it picks up the whole configuration. One config, many placements.
- It stays in your org. Nothing is stored on a vendor server, so the configuration is yours and it is visible in Setup.

### Import, export, and the mapping step people miss
The Import / Export tab takes a JSON configuration and turns it into a saved config. That is how the Config Library works: 40+ ready-made configurations covering time-off requests, room booking, hot-desking, interview scheduling, fleet reservation and more.
The step that saves the most time is Smart Field Mapping. Library configs reference the demo objects; your org has its own. The wizard scans every reference the moment you paste, flags each one your org does not have, and puts a dropdown next to it sourced live from the object's real field list. Remap in the wizard, click Apply, and it deploys with the rewritten JSON. No text editor, no hunt and replace, no re-uploads.
Export works the same way in reverse, which makes configurations shareable. A config that works in one org is a paste away from working in another.

### Using the config once it exists
Drop any of the three components onto a Lightning record page, app page, Home page or Experience Cloud site, set Config Name to the name you chose, and leave every other property blank. The config supplies them. On App, Home and Experience pages, put the parent record in Static Parent Record Id.
The same applies inside a Screen Flow: put the config's name in Config Name and every on/off setting comes from the config. You do not set a single checkbox in Flow Builder; the few flow-only ones (Required, Show Inline, Output Date Ranges as JSON) are off unless you turn them on. Pass the parent record into Parent Record Id.

## Calendar Time Slot Picker for Salesforce, No Code (/blog/salesforce-calendar-time-slot-picker.html)

A Salesforce time slot picker: a calendar with bookable slots at any interval, taken times hidden before anyone clicks, live capacity counts, and no code.

Salesforce gives you a date picker and a time field. It does not give you a grid of selectable slots. Here is what a real Salesforce time slot picker takes, and how to get one without building it.
A time slot picker is a specific interface: a calendar where you choose a day, and a grid underneath showing that day broken into bookable intervals, with the taken ones visibly unavailable. Everyone recognizes it, because every booking site on the internet uses it. Salesforce does not ship one.

### What Salesforce actually gives you
A standard Date/Time field renders as a date input plus a time dropdown. It is a form control, and it has no idea what else is booked. Nothing stops a user selecting a slot that is already gone, because the field does not know other records exist. That check happens later, in a validation rule or a flow, after the user has already committed to a choice.
That is the gap. A time slot picker queries existing records before the user chooses, and only offers what is free.

### What a real slot picker has to do

### Why building it yourself is more work than it looks
The rendering is the easy part. These are the parts nobody scopes:
- **Querying bookings**
Efficiently, without blowing governor limits when someone opens a two-month view.
- **Overlap math**
Fiddly the moment bookings can be different lengths.
- **Timezones**
The running user's timezone and the record's are not always the same.
- **Race conditions**
Two people looking at the same free slot at the same moment.
- **Field-level security**
The component has to respect what the running user can see.
- **Accessibility**
A grid of clickable divs is not keyboard navigable by default.
Accessibility needs the most care. A slot grid needs proper ARIA grid semantics, arrow-key navigation, and a state that is conveyed by more than color. It is the part most in-house builds skip, and the part a procurement review asks about.

### Grouping slots so people can actually scan them
A 9-to-5 day at 15 minute intervals is 32 slots. Presented as a flat list, that is a wall. Grouping by period (morning, afternoon, evening) turns it into three short blocks. That helps most when the person choosing is a customer on a phone.

### When you do not need the calendar at all
Sometimes the date is already implied. On a record page for an appointment that already has a date, a month calendar is redundant. Time Grid Only drops the calendar and shows just the slot grid for that one date, taken from a field on the host record or set directly.

### The settings that make the picker
Each one is a field in the Setup Wizard. Nothing here needs code.

### Questions people ask
Q: What is a calendar time slot picker?
A calendar where you choose a day, with a grid underneath that splits the day into bookable intervals. Slots that are already taken are shown as unavailable, so people only pick times that are free.
Q: Does Salesforce have a time slot picker?
Not for your own objects. A standard Date/Time field is a date input plus a time dropdown, and it cannot see other records. MultiDatePick adds a time slot picker that reads existing bookings when the calendar loads and only offers what is free.
Q: Can the time slots be any length?
Yes. The slot interval is any number of minutes. 15, 30 or 60 minutes are typical, and a 45 minute interview slot works the same way.
Q: Do I need Apex or a developer to add a time slot picker?
No. The Setup Wizard writes the configuration, and the component goes on a record page, app page, Experience Cloud site or Screen Flow by setting Config Name. There is no code to write.

## Five Calendar Views, One Salesforce Component (/blog/salesforce-calendar-views.html)

A month grid cannot answer every scheduling question. Timeline, week, utilization and agenda alongside it, chosen per placement with one config field.

A month grid is the wrong shape for half the scheduling questions people actually ask. Here is why we added four more views, and how choosing between them became a config field instead of a rebuild.
Every calendar starts as a month grid, because that is what the word makes you picture. Then people start asking questions it cannot answer. "Who is free Thursday afternoon?" "Is Room 4 booked solid next week?" "Which technician is over capacity?" The grid holds all of that data. It just makes you hunt for it.
MultiDatePick now renders the same records five ways. One component, one set of field mappings, one save path, and a View setting that changes the layout.

### The five views, and the question each one answers
Each view is built for one question. Same records underneath, drawn the way that question needs.
- **What is happening on the 14th?**
A month at a time, each day filled with the status of what is booked on it. Days that mix statuses get diagonal stripes. The default, and still the right answer most of the time.
- **Which resource is free, and when?**
Resources down the side, dates across the top. A booking that spans three days draws as one bar, overlapping bookings stack into lanes, and a capacity strip shows how full each day is. Zoom from a single day to a whole month, and drag a bar to move or stretch it. More on the Timeline view.
- **Who is free Thursday at 2pm?**
Seven days across, business hours down, each booking sized to its real length. Bookings that overlap sit side by side in their own status colors, and the strip beside them stays open so you can add one more.
- **Who is over capacity?**
Booked against capacity, per resource per day, on one blue scale. Overbooked days get an orange ring, and a combined row sums the team. Click any cell to drop into that resource's week. More on the utilization heatmap.
- **What is next?**
A flat list of the next 60 days, grouped by date, with the times, statuses and fields you pick. Reads well on a phone and in a shift handover.
Utilization and Agenda are read only by design: they answer a question rather than take a booking. The other three are fully interactive.

### Five views, one definition of a booking
The usual version of this story ends with a second component: its own fields, its own save logic, its own bugs. Here all five views read the same records through the same field mappings, honor the same conflict rules and blocked dates, and write through the same save path. Switching from Calendar to Timeline cannot change what a booking means, because there is only one definition of a booking.
Two settings control it:
- **View**
Which layout the component opens on: Calendar, Timeline, Week, Utilization or Agenda.
- **Available Views**
The views the switcher offers. Leave it blank to offer all five, or narrow it to the two that make sense for this page.
So one component becomes three different tools. A recruiter's Interview Scheduling page opens on Week, because interviews are a time-of-day problem. A facilities manager's Room Booking page opens on Calendar with Timeline and Utilization alongside, because rooms are a capacity problem. A wall display opens on Agenda and offers nothing writable at all.

### Choose the view per placement
An org-wide calendar setting is close to useless, because one company is not asking one question. Sales wants next week. Operations wants next quarter. A shift manager wants today, by the hour. Finance wants a utilization number.
View is set on each placement of the component. Put MultiDatePick on four record pages, a Flow screen, a Home page and a public Experience Cloud site, and each can be a different view of the same objects. No second install, no field mappings to keep in sync.
Timeline has two settings of its own:
When one resource has several overlapping bookings, its row collapses to a single strip with a count, and expands on click into one lane per booking. Density becomes something the user chooses rather than something the data inflicts on them.

### Point the resource lookup at User and it becomes people scheduling
The resource lookup points at any object. Rooms gives you room booking. Equipment gives you checkout. Point it at User and every view above becomes a staffing tool: Timeline is a roster, Week is a shift grid, Utilization is a team capacity dashboard. Managers ask "who is over capacity" about people far more often than about rooms.
There are two ready-made configs for exactly this in the library: Team Capacity Planning, which opens on the Utilization heatmap, and Staff Shift Roster, which opens on Timeline. Both use User as the resource.

### Every config in the library now ships with a view already chosen
Picking a default view is a judgment call, and it is easier to copy one than to make one. So every config in the Config Library now specifies both a default view and a switcher list, chosen for what each config is actually for:
Import any of them, remap the field names to your own schema, and the view choice comes along with it.

- Views and look: calendar, timeline, week, utilization heatmap and agenda (FullCalendar's timeline is Premium and it has no utilization view), Timeline Group By Field, Edit Mode for many records at once, Button Label, Calendar Title, Calendar Size, Two-Month View, Week Starts on Monday.
